title: Partition merge trusts the peer's HostCompare.connected, .score and self-signed epoch, so any member can take over a live host
scenario: M is a member connected to honest host H, which has N members. M signs its own HostClaim{epoch: H.epoch+1000} and sends Ctl::HostCompare{claim, connected: 1000, score: 9999} on its member link. compare_from_member (host.rs:873-891) only checks the signature and that claim.host == sender. my_side counts H's links minus M, so merge_winner(sent, theirs) is false and H goes to AwaitMember{M}. M then sends HostMoved{claim with a higher epoch, addr}. member_frame (host.rs:798-818) calls lose_merge_links (host.rs:663-675), which relays HostMoved to every member and closes them with CLOSE_REDIRECT. Every member (member.rs:227-253) and H itself seek and join M. M now holds the roster, ack and censorship, all plaintext media, and the power to feed divergent histories. The same works as the probed side: probe_frame (host.rs:897-917) trusts the HostCompare M sends after answering H's probe dial with a Welcome. H probes peers named by the rdv record, which M can write, by mDNS and by cached peers. M can also spam HostCompare and lose on purpose. Each one forces win_merge (host.rs:640-660): a new claim signature, upsert_conv and a HostMoved broadcast to all members. Nothing rate-limits this.
fix: 1) core: add Attestation{server, host, epoch, member, issued_ms}, signed by the member over "tincan-attest1" || postcard(att). Append Ctl::Attest(SignedAttestation) and Ctl::HostCompare2{claim, attests: Vec<SignedAttestation> (max 64)} at the end of Ctl. Treat the legacy HostCompare as 0 verified members. 2) Member: send Attest to the current host after Welcome, after every HostMoved (including a same-host epoch refresh) and every 60 s. 3) Host: keep the latest valid Attest per MLink (member == link.peer, host == me, epoch == my claim epoch, issued within 120 s, signature ok) and drop it in drop_member. 4) On receipt, count only attestations that verify, name the sender as host with the sender's claim epoch, were issued within 180 s, come from ConvState::is_member users, are unique, and are neither me, the sender, nor in my links. My own count is my stored valid attests excluding the peer. Compute merge_winner on (verified_count, epoch, Reverse(host)) and drop the self-reported score from the key. 5) Safety rule: never enter AwaitMember/AwaitProbe when the peer's verified count <= my connected links excluding the peer. Disagreement then only delays a merge (both win: the split stays until the next probe; both lose: merge_timeout). It can never move members. 6) Ignore claims with epoch > epoch_seen + MAX_EPOCH_JUMP (see E1). Accept at most one compare per peer per 60 s, and after winning ignore further compares from that peer until its link closes. Residual risks to document: two hosts with 0 verified members still compare by epoch and id, which is equivalent to 'online first' because neither loses attested members. Sybils remain possible: any member can mint invites and admit throwaway identities through the honest host, and each one attests for free. Optional hardening: count only attesters admitted at least 1 h before the compare. A rogue host can still keep members it already holds by ignoring a lost merge.
verdict: Could not refute; this violates must-not #1. compare_from_member (session/host.rs:873-891) checks only that no merge or handoff is running, that the claim signature is valid, and that claim.host == sender. `connected` and `score` are used as sent, and merge_winner sorts by connected first (tincan-core election.rs:171-173). Any member can sign a claim naming itself. Once H is in AwaitMember{M}, member_frame HostMoved (host.rs:798-818) needs only a self-signed claim with a higher epoch. lose_merge_links then relays HostMoved and closes every member with CLOSE_REDIRECT (host.rs:663-675). host_moved (member.rs:227-253) sends each member to dial M, and M can answer with its own Welcome. Nothing re-checks Hello, roster or membership on the way. probe_frame (host.rs:897-917) trusts the probed side's HostCompare in the same way. Spam path: after a win, h.merge is None again (host.rs:886-887, 906-913), so M can repeat at once. Each round costs a claim signature, an upsert_conv through update_record, N HostMoved sends and an epoch bump. Nothing rate-limits it.
refined_fix: Now, no wire change: (a) Yield rule in compare_from_member and probe_frame. A host enters AwaitMember/AwaitProbe only when it has 0 connected members besides the peer AND key(peer) > key(me), with key = (claimed connected, epoch, Reverse(host)). When both sides have at least 1 member, neither yields and neither calls win_merge: close the probe link. Both sides compute the same outcome, so it stays antisymmetric. Solo-vs-solo and solo-vs-populated merges keep working. Two populated partitions stop merging automatically. They still exchange history over the probe link at every probe (SyncHave both ways, host.rs:634 and 937-940, every 5 min), and they rejoin when one host leaves. Document this. (b) Allow at most one compare per peer per 60 s. After winning, ignore further compares from that peer until its link closes. (c) Apply the epoch bound from E1 in both compare paths. Follow-up, wire change: member-signed Attestation{server, host, epoch, member, issued_ms}. Count only attestations that verify, are at most 180 s old, are unique, come from ConvState::is_member users, and are not from me, the sender or my own links. Put the verified count in place of the claimed connected, drop score from the key, and keep the rule 'never yield when the peer's verified count <= my connected'. Bounding Sybil attesters needs N20's admission limits (optionally: attesters admitted at least 1 h earlier). Residual: a rogue host can refuse to yield and keep its own members.

title: Welcome.your_next_seq from the host is trusted, so a malicious host can permanently silence a member
scenario: M is the host (it was online first). Honest X connects, and M's Welcome carries your_next_seq = 1<<60, stored as MemberState.next_seq_hint (member.rs:53). X's next publish calls sign_own(body, next_seq_hint) (mod.rs:1121). sign_own takes seq = next_own_seq.max(seq_hint) = 1<<60 (mod.rs:1252). The local check returns Gap, not Reject, so the event is signed and reserve_own_seq persists own_floor = 1<<60 (replica.rs:113-119). From then on every event X authors in that server, through any honest host, carries seq >= 1<<60 and is a Gap on every honest replica forever. A 'gap' answer only lowers the floor by one (replica.rs:125-131), and the floor survives leave and re-join on purpose. X can never post in that server again from this profile.
fix: Never let the host raise my seq. Ignore your_next_seq, or use it only when it is <= next_own_seq. Before the first publish on a new host link, also wait for the host's initial sync to me (m.synced, set on the empty Events{more:false}). My own events that the host holds are signed by me and verifiable, so they advance state.next_seq(me) legitimately. Optionally, sign_own should refuse a seq above max(state.next_seq(me), own_floor + 1).
verdict: Could not refute. Welcome.your_next_seq is copied unchecked into MemberStart.next_seq (mod.rs:655-668, 1218-1221), then into MemberState.next_seq_hint (member.rs:47-53). pump_publishes calls sign_own(body, m.next_seq_hint) (mod.rs:1121). sign_own takes seq = next_own_seq.max(seq_hint) (mod.rs:1252). state.check runs in Live mode, so a far-ahead seq is a Gap, not a Reject (state.rs:576-578, 428). The event is signed and reserve_own_seq persists own_floor = 1<<60 (replica.rs:113-119). From then on next_own_seq = max(head + 1, floor + 1) (replica.rs:110). Honest hosts answer 'gap'. After 5 retries reject_inflight releases only that one seq (member.rs:213-218, replica.rs:125-131), so the next event carries about 1<<60 again. The floor is kept across leave and re-join on purpose. Result: the author can never post in that server from this profile, through any host. That is permanent disruption of an honest member's session, far beyond what a bad link could cause.
refined_fix: Ignore your_next_seq: call sign_own(body, 0) in pump_publishes and remove next_seq_hint. In the member branch of pump_publishes, also wait for m.synced (set on the host's terminal empty Events, member.rs:118-127), not only m.sync_out_done. That way my own signed events that the host holds arrive and advance state.next_seq(me) before I sign. A host that never sends the marker can only censor me, which it can do anyway. As a defence, make sign_own refuse seq > max(state.next_seq(me), own_floor + 1). Recovery for already-poisoned profiles: on Replica::load, if own_floor > state.next_seq(me) + 1_000_000, reset it to state.head(me). Events signed that far ahead can never become applicable, so reusing lower seqs is safe.

title: Unthrottled fan-out (Typing, Publish, Status) overflows honest members' live queues, and the host then disconnects them as 'too slow'
scenario: M sends Ctl::Typing{channel, by: M} in a tight loop: about 70 bytes each, 20k per second, roughly 1.4 MB/s. The host checks by == M and broadcasts every frame to all N-1 members with try_send on a 1024-frame live queue (host.rs:790-795, link.rs:32,257). The host's uplink cannot carry N x 1.4 MB/s, so queues fill within a fraction of a second and broadcast() closes each such member with 'too slow' (host.rs:229-232). Each dropped member treats this as host loss (member.rs:79-85, host_lost). S1 then promotes itself at once (rank 0), which splits the server and causes merges and full resyncs for as long as the flood lasts. A stream of valid Publish events (each fanned out, host.rs:739-750) or Status churn (a roster broadcast every 250 ms, host.rs:767-771) works the same way. Every Typing frame is also re-emitted to the host's UI.
fix: Add per-member token buckets on the host before any fan-out. Typing: at most 1 per 2 s per (member, channel); drop or coalesce the rest. Status: at most 1 per 2 s, coalesced. Publish: e.g. 5/s with a burst of 20; above that, stop reading that member's frames briefly (backpressure) or answer with a retryable reason the member treats like 'gap' (see N9 so seqs are never released). In broadcast(), when the queue is full, drop ephemeral frames (Typing, Roster, Tick, VvDigest, HostMoved refresh) instead of closing the member. Close only when a non-droppable Events frame has failed to queue continuously for more than 2 s.
verdict: Could not refute. The only check on Typing is by == sender. Each frame is then broadcast to all other members and emitted to the host UI (host.rs:790-795). broadcast() uses try_send on the 1024-frame live queue and closes any member whose queue is full with CLOSE_NORMAL 'too slow' (host.rs:223-233; link.rs:32, 249-257). The member treats that close as host loss (member.rs:79-85 -> host_lost), and S1 promotes at once at rank 0 (mod.rs:984, 1000-1001), which splits the server. Nothing rate-limits Typing, Status (each one calls mark_roster; the roster then goes out every 250 ms, host.rs:767-771) or Publish fan-out (host.rs:739-750). A flood also takes up the session-wide LINK_QUEUE (mod.rs:327), which delays every other member's frames. The disconnect-as-punishment step is where the amplification comes from.
refined_fix: Add per-member token buckets on the host before any fan-out. Typing: at most 1 per 2 s per (member, channel); drop the rest. Status: coalesce, keep the latest and apply at most every 2 s (the 250 ms roster debounce stays). Publish: for example 5/s with a burst of 20. Above that, pause reading that link briefly, or answer with a retryable refusal; that needs N9's never-release rule so seqs are not released. In broadcast(), when a queue is full, drop droppable frames (Typing, Roster, Tick, VvDigest, a same-host HostMoved refresh, SoundPlayed) instead of closing. Close only when an Events frame cannot be queued for more than 2 s, or mark that link for resync. Give each link a frames-per-second budget in its reader task so one member cannot take over the shared link_tx queue.

title: tincan/dm/1 accepts any stranger: unbounded DM conversations, replicas, pending buffers and rings
scenario: A non-member who knows my UserId generates K fresh ed25519 keys. My id appears in every roster I am in and in 'Copy my ID'. From each key it dials tincan/dm/1 with DmHello{conv: ConvId::dm(me, key)}. The only check is that conv is the hash of the pair (dm.rs:441). open_conv then upserts a ConvRecord on disk, builds a Replica with its own PendingBuffer, inserts a DmPeer, spawns a Link and run_conn, and emits DmOpened (dm.rs:343-377, 445-455). Each stranger then sends Events with its own validly signed messages at seq 2..10001, withholding seq 1. They pass the party check and are Live-mode Gaps (state.rs:573-577), so they are buffered up to MAX_PENDING_EVENTS / 32 MiB per conversation (state.rs:98-100). K strangers x 32 MiB is unbounded memory, plus K rows on disk and a flooded DM list. Each stranger can also ring me with CallInvite (hub.rs:342-359). No MAC or membership check gates this ALPN, contrary to the threat-model assumption that non-members fail at the door.
fix: Treat unknown peers (not an existing DM contact and not a member of any shared server) as requests. Do not call open_conv or upsert_conv until they deliver one valid in-order event. Keep at most about 16 pending requests in memory with LRU eviction and store nothing else. For DM replicas use a much smaller pending cap (e.g. 64 events / 256 KiB), and drop Gap events from strangers entirely. Rate-limit incoming DM connections per peer and globally (e.g. 10 per minute). Ignore CallInvite from non-contacts unless the user opted in.
verdict: Could not refute. DmProto (proto.rs:77-90) hands every tincan/dm/1 connection to accept_incoming. Its only checks are conv == ConvId::dm(me, peer) and peer != me (dm.rs:441). open_conv then writes a ConvRecord, builds a Replica with its own PendingBuffer, inserts it into net.replicas and emits DmOpened (dm.rs:343-377). register adds a DmPeer and spawns a Link and run_conn (dm.rs:268-316). There is no per-peer or global cap and no rate limit. The stranger is a DM party, so its own events at seq 2.. with seq 1 withheld pass the party check and are Live Gaps (state.rs:573-577), buffered up to 10,000 events / 32 MiB per conversation (state.rs:98-100, 862-881). K fresh keys mean K x 32 MiB held while the app runs, K rows on disk and K DM list entries. The notes say accepting strangers is intended (notes-tincan-net.md:35), but unbounded state per stranger is not. CallInvite rings are limited to one at a time, because a second caller gets busy (hub.rs:338-341), so ringing is only an annoyance.
refined_fix: Treat unknown peers (no existing DM conversation and not a member of any shared server) as requests. Do not call open_conv or upsert_conv until they deliver one valid event that applies in order. Keep at most about 16 pending requests in memory with LRU eviction and store nothing else. Never buffer Gap events from them. For DM replicas use a much smaller pending cap (for example 64 events / 256 KiB). Rate-limit incoming DM connections per peer and globally (for example 10 per minute). Ignore CallInvite from non-contacts unless the user opted in.

title: A malicious successor can block failover forever by answering 'alive, not hosting'
scenario: M ranks S1: it has a direct path and reports Status{ac_power: true, uptime_s: 7200} (see N13). The honest host crashes or leaves, or M ignores a Handoff so the host times out and closes with HOST_LEAVING. M never promotes. It answers every Hello with Reject{NotHost}, or with a Redirect to the dead host carrying its old claim (mod.rs:733-740). Each 1 s redial refreshes alive_above through note_alive_not_host (mod.rs:698-710). seek_timer then pushes the deadline back by one stagger, forever, for lower-ranked successors (mod.rs:929-931) and for non-successors (mod.rs:946-949, which never fall back to cold open). Seeking members reject each other's Hellos (mod.rs:829-831). Nobody hosts the server while M stays online.
fix: Let 'alive but not hosting' postpone promotion at most once per higher-ranked successor. Record when each one was first seen alive and ignore it after 2 x stagger, treating it as failed for this failover and removing it from the local succession. For non-successors, cap the total wait at the original deadline plus one stagger, then cold open. An honest S1 promotes at once (rank 0), so this costs honest runs nothing.
verdict: Could not refute; a malicious S1 holds the server hostless while it stays online. note_alive_not_host refreshes alive_above whenever a higher-ranked successor answers Reject{NotHost} (mod.rs:685-687, 698-710), or sends a Redirect to the failed host with its old claim (mod.rs:733-740). It also schedules a 1 s redial (failover_redial). seek_timer pushes the deadline back by one stagger whenever alive_above is younger than the stagger (3 s), with no cap. That covers ranked successors (mod.rs:928-932) and non-successors, who therefore never reach the cold open (mod.rs:945-950). Failover seekers reject each other's Hellos (mod.rs:829-831). S1 itself is not affected (rank 0 has nobody above), so M must be S1, which it can be (see N13). Not handling a Handoff gives the same result through the CLOSE_HOST_LEAVING failover. An honest S1 behind a bad link would fail to answer the dial and so would not block anyone.
refined_fix: In Seek, record when each higher-ranked successor was first seen 'alive, not hosting' during this failover. After host_dead + stagger (about 13 s; host_dead allows for an honest successor that has not yet noticed the loss), ignore further alive notices from it, remove it from the local succession and stop treating it as above me. For rank None, cap the total wait at the original deadline + host_dead + stagger, then cold open (the cold-open race then elects the lower id). An honest S1 promotes at rank 0 at once, so honest runs are not slowed.

title: KeyframeRequest and Subscribe re-seed the whole GOP cache without a rate limit (up to 2 MiB per 5-byte frame)
scenario: M subscribes to a live share, then sends Ctl::KeyframeRequest{track}, or repeats Subscribe{track}, hundreds of times per second. While the cache is fresh (under 1.5 s), viewer_wants_key flushes M's viewer and enqueues the whole cached group again, up to 2 MiB (track.rs:424-444). Each Subscribe goes through Sfu::on_ctl (sfu.rs:464-476) to add_remote (track.rs:382-396), which spawns a new writer and uni stream seeded with the full cache. The replaced viewer's writer keeps writing its remaining queue. With a fast downlink, M soaks the host's uplink, so every member's voice datagrams and every other viewer's video from this host degrade. An honest viewer asks at most once per second (voice.rs:528-540).
fix: In Sfu::on_ctl, ignore Subscribe when members[member].subs already contains the track (no re-add). In add_remote, keep an existing viewer instead of replacing it. In VideoTrack, keep a per-viewer last_seed Instant and allow at most one re-seed per KEYFRAME_EVERY (1 s). Otherwise just mark the viewer want_key and use the coalesced upstream request. Allow one writer task per (viewer, track).
verdict: Could not refute. hub.on_ctl passes member frames to Sfu::on_ctl with no filter (hub.rs:263-269; hooks.rs:60-77). Subscribe never checks whether the member is already subscribed (sfu.rs:464-476). add_remote always spawns a new writer and seeds it with the whole cached group, up to 2 MiB or 4 s, without a freshness check (track.rs:382-396, 482-493). It replaces the old viewer, whose dropped sender lets the old writer finish its queued group (track.rs:535-552). So N Subscribes give N parallel up-to-2 MiB group writes. KeyframeRequest with a fresh cache flushes and re-seeds the viewer (track.rs:424-444). With a stale cache it causes an upstream IDR at most once per second, which keeps the cache fresh. Honest viewers ask at most once per second (voice.rs:528-540) and subscribe once. How much this hurts other members' media depends on how the shared bottleneck splits between per-connection congestion controllers (estimate; not measured).
refined_fix: In Sfu::on_ctl Subscribe, return early when m.subs already contains the track. In VideoTrack::add_remote, keep an existing ViewerId::Peer viewer instead of replacing it, so there is one writer per (viewer, track). Give each remote viewer a last_seed Instant and allow at most one re-seed per KEYFRAME_EVERY (1 s, the honest rate). Otherwise only set want_key and rely on the coalesced upstream request.

title: Member uplink media is not rate-limited: an audio datagram flood drowns the room, and video uploads ignore TargetBitrate
scenario: M joins a voice room and sends about 1,200-byte datagrams with its own valid voice track id at 5,000/s (6 MB/s). forward() copies each one to every room member's connection (sfu.rs:381-394), which has only a 16 KiB datagram send buffer each (config.rs:82), and to the host engine's audio_in (256-entry try_send). Honest members' 50 packets/s voice is crowded out of every receiver's buffer and of the host's queue, and the host's uplink is multiplied by room size minus one. For video, Upload::frame (sfu.rs:643-648) never checks M's input against its TargetBitrate. M can upload 50 Mbps of frames, and the SFU pushes them to every subscriber. Per-viewer drop policy bounds queues, not the host's total uplink.
fix: In forward_task, give each member a token bucket for packets (e.g. 100/s, burst 20) and bytes (e.g. 256 kbit/s), and drop datagrams larger than AUDIO_HEADER_LEN + 1,275 bytes (the Opus maximum) before forwarding. In Upload::frame, apply a token bucket at 1.5 x the track's current AIMD target, with a burst of one keyframe up to 1 MiB. On overflow, drop the frame and call t.gap() so viewers skip to the next keyframe.
verdict: Could not refute. forward_task reads all of a member's datagrams (sfu.rs:659-669). forward() drops only datagrams whose track id is not the sender's own voice track. It copies every other datagram to every room member's connection and try_sends it to the host's audio_in (sfu.rs:366-395). There is no packet, byte or size limit. Each receiving connection has a 16 KiB datagram send buffer (config.rs:82), so a 100x flood displaces honest 50 pkt/s voice in every receiver's buffer and in the host engine's queue. The exact eviction policy is the transport's (hedged: oldest-first in quinn-style stacks). Host uplink use is multiplied by room size minus one. For video, Upload::frame pushes every frame (sfu.rs:643-648). The per-viewer drop budget scales with the measured input rate (track.rs:161-164, 319), so an over-rate source is forwarded at whatever each viewer's congestion window allows. Honest sharers stay at or below 4.5 Mbps because their encoder caps it.
refined_fix: In forward_task, give each member a token bucket: about 100 packets/s with a burst of 20, and about 256 kbit/s. Drop datagrams longer than AUDIO_HEADER_LEN + 1275 (the Opus maximum) before forwarding. In Upload::frame, apply a token bucket at 1.5 x VIDEO_MAX_BPS as a hard cap, plus one keyframe burst of up to 2 MiB. Optionally use a tighter bucket at 1.5 x the current AIMD target with a 4 s lag allowance, so an honest encoder that is still adapting is not hit. On overflow, drop the frame and call t.gap() so viewers skip to the next keyframe.

title: Every SyncHave spawns a new full-history send_missing task (unbounded tasks and memory)
scenario: M sends Ctl::SyncHave{heads: Heads(vec![])} 10,000 times, about 10 bytes each. Each one spawns send_missing (mod.rs:1231-1242), which plans the whole history and reads it from storage. All of them block on the 2-slot bulk queue (link.rs:34), each holding a filled 256 KiB page: roughly 2.5 GB of memory plus 10,000 storage scans on the host. The same unbounded spawn exists on probe links (host.rs:937-940), on members for SyncHave from a host (member.rs:130-132), and on DM links for SyncHave and in-stream DmHello from any DM peer (dm.rs:493-503, 529, 536).
fix: Allow at most one send_missing in flight per link. Store the latest received heads in the link state, and when LinkEvent::SyncSent arrives, run once more only if newer heads were stored. Also allow at most one full resync per link per 10 s. In dm::run_conn, keep an in-flight flag plus pending heads in the same way.
verdict: Could not refute. Every SyncHave from a member calls spawn_sync unconditionally (host.rs:757-758). The same happens on probe links (host.rs:937-940), on members for a SyncHave from the host (member.rs:130-132), and on DM links for SyncHave and in-stream DmHello whenever something is missing (dm.rs:493-503, 529, 536). Each task plans the whole difference, reads it from storage and blocks in bulk.send on a 2-slot queue while holding a filled page (replica.rs:150-209; link.rs:34). A peer that does not read keeps every task blocked. 10,000 tiny SyncHave(empty) frames give 10,000 tasks, each holding up to about 256 KiB plus its encoded copy, and 10,000 storage scans (estimate: about 2.5 GB or more once history exceeds one page). Honest peers send SyncHave on connect and at most about every 30 s.
refined_fix: Allow at most one send_missing in flight per link. Store the latest received heads in the link state, and on LinkEvent::SyncSent run once more only if newer heads arrived in the meantime. Allow at most one full resync per link per 10 s (the honest digest-driven rate is at most once per 30 s). Do the same in dm::run_conn (an in-flight flag plus pending heads). Optionally cap concurrent send_missing tasks per session.

title: Video receive path buffers up to 8 MiB per stream across about 100 concurrent streams, and pending groups are unbounded
scenario: Any member can do this: add_member starts spawn_video_rx for every member, with no voice room needed (sfu.rs:165). M opens about 100 uni streams, the QUIC default, each with a valid header for its own screen track (Upload::accept). On each it sends a varint length of 8 MiB followed by 8 MiB - 1 bytes. VideoFrameReader keeps each partial frame in app memory (MAX_VIDEO_FRAME = 8 MiB, tincan-core media.rs:201), and QUIC credit is returned as it reads, so this reaches about 800 MiB per connection. Separately, after one valid keyframe group whose stream M never ends, M sends one frame each on streams with ever-new group_seq values. Each creates a fresh Pending entry (recv.rs:254-262): it is under 200 ms old and under 60 frames, so it is never switched or evicted, and pending grows without bound. The same code runs on members for host streams and in calls.
fix: Lower MAX_VIDEO_FRAME to 2 MiB (the GOP cache bound). Cap concurrent read_stream tasks per connection at about 4, stopping the oldest with VIDEO_REFUSED. Cap pending groups per track at 2 (on a third, switch to the newest or drop the oldest) and pending bytes per track at about 4 MiB. Check the oldest pending group's age on every message, not only on the group just pushed.
verdict: Could not refute. add_member starts spawn_video_rx for every member link, with no voice room needed (sfu.rs:162-167). video_rx spawns a reader for each accepted uni stream, with no cap of its own (recv.rs:85-101). Only the header has a timeout (recv.rs:104-123). VideoFrameReader keeps partial frames up to MAX_VIDEO_FRAME = 8 MiB in app memory (tincan-core media.rs:201-233), and read_chunk returns QUIC credit as it reads. About 100 concurrent streams (the transport default, hedged) x 8 MiB is roughly 800 MiB per connection (estimate). Pending groups: a new, newer group while the current group is unfinished and not waiting for a key gets a fresh Pending entry (recv.rs:251-262). Only the group just pushed is checked for age or size, so one frame per new group, on short streams that M finishes, never triggers a switch or eviction. Pending grows without bound. The same code runs for host streams on members and in calls.
refined_fix: Lower MAX_VIDEO_FRAME to 2 MiB, which matches the GOP cache bound; encoder input is at most 1920 wide. Cap concurrent read_stream tasks per connection at about 4, stopping new streams with VIDEO_REFUSED. Add an idle timeout per stream (for example: no complete frame within 2 s means stop). Cap pending groups per track at 2 (on a third, switch to the newest or drop the oldest) and pending bytes per track at about 4 MiB. Check the oldest pending group's age on every message, not only that of the group just pushed.

title: Self-signed epochs and the unsigned Hello.epoch_seen are unbounded: overflow panics or wraps, and epochs get poisoned permanently
scenario: (a) Cold-open race: M, with a higher UserId, sends a valid Hello with epoch_seen = u64::MAX (an unsigned field) to seeking member X. X computes epoch_seen.max(their_epoch) + 1 (mod.rs:811). Workspace crates keep overflow checks in dev builds, so this panics there and kills X's session actor; in release it wraps to 0. (b) M hosts legitimately once and signs a claim with epoch u64::MAX. Every member sets epoch_seen to it (mod.rs:661, member.rs:232) and persists last_epoch (update_record, mod.rs:1311-1320). Every later promotion computes epoch_seen + 1 (mod.rs:910, 933; member.rs:266; host.rs:642 in win_merge), which panics or wraps to epoch 0. After that, honest hosts lose every epoch comparison to M's stale claim: the merge key (election.rs:172) and the rdv clobber rule (rdv.rs:341). This is also reachable through compare_from_member (host.rs:883) and probe_frame (host.rs:905).
fix: Use checked_add everywhere an epoch is incremented, and refuse to claim on overflow. Ignore any claim whose epoch > epoch_seen + MAX_EPOCH_JUMP (e.g. 1,000,000): in on_dial Welcome, on_redirect, host_moved, Handoff, HostCompare and the cold-open race. Never persist such an epoch in update_record. Do not use Hello.epoch_seen for epoch selection at all; use only verified claims.
verdict: Could not refute. [profile.release] does not enable overflow-checks (Cargo.toml:63-69), so `+ 1` on u64::MAX wraps to 0 in release builds. In dev builds it panics the session task. Epochs from peers are never bounded. Hello.epoch_seen is outside the MAC (mod.rs:794-811). A Welcome claim raises epoch_seen (mod.rs:661), and become_member persists it as last_epoch (mod.rs:1010-1011, 1311-1320). compare_from_member (host.rs:883) and probe_frame (host.rs:905) raise epoch_seen from a self-signed claim, so any member, not only a host, can push H's epoch_seen to u64::MAX with one HostCompare claiming connected 0. H then wins and win_merge (host.rs:642) wraps to epoch 0. Members ignore that HostMoved (member.rs:229) and every later Roster (member.rs:112 needs r.epoch >= m.claim.epoch), so their succession and short ids go stale. With last_epoch = u64::MAX persisted, every later promotion (mod.rs:910, 933; member.rs:266) claims 0. The checks `epoch > current` (host.rs:799, 922; member.rs:229) then fail, so merges and handoff acks can never complete. This survives restarts.
refined_fix: Use checked_add at every increment: mod.rs:407, 811, 910, 933; member.rs:266; host.rs:642. On overflow, refuse to claim. Add MAX_EPOCH_JUMP (for example 1_000_000; honest epochs grow by 1 per migration). Ignore any claim with epoch > epoch_seen + MAX_EPOCH_JUMP in on_dial Welcome, welcome_start, on_redirect, host_moved, accept_handoff, member_frame HostMoved, compare_from_member and probe_frame. Never raise epoch_seen or call update_record from a claim that was not accepted. Stop using Hello.epoch_seen to choose the epoch in the cold-open race; use only epoch_seen from verified claims, or clamp it the same way. Recovery: on load, treat last_epoch > u64::MAX - MAX_EPOCH_JUMP as corrupt and reset it to 0.

title: A rejected PublishAck releases a signed seq, so a malicious host can make an honest member equivocate; the reason text is shown verbatim
scenario: M is the host. Honest X publishes event A (X, seq n). M stores A and fans it out to some members, but answers PublishAck{ok: false, reason: "gap"} five times (or any other reason once). reject_inflight releases seq n (member.rs:213-224, replica.rs:125-131). X's next message B is signed with the same seq n, and M acks B. X has now signed two events for (X, n). Replicas that received A keep A; X and the others keep B. Each replica keeps the first it saw, and heads-only sync never notices, so X's history diverges across honest members and X looks like an equivocator. The reason string, up to about 1 MiB, also reaches the user verbatim through NetError::Rejected, which allows phishing text.
fix: Never release a seq whose signed event has left the device. On ok:false, keep the same signed event in inflight (no re-signing), stop retrying on this link, and resend it after the next Welcome from any host. Release the seq only when the local state also Rejects that exact event (re-run state.check on it). Map host reasons to a fixed set of user messages, or truncate to 200 chars and strip control characters.
verdict: Could not refute; this violates the 'honest members must not diverge' must-not. Any PublishAck ok:false other than 'gap', or 'gap' answered 5 times, calls reject_inflight. That releases the seq (member.rs:198-224; replica.rs:125-131) even though the signed event has already left the device. The next event is signed with the same (author, seq). A malicious host can store or fan out event A, refuse it, then ack event B. Replicas keep whichever arrived first (state.rs:567-569, Stale), and heads-only sync never notices (N10), so X's history forks and X looks like an equivocator. The notes record this only for the crash case (notes-tincan-net.md:162). The reason string comes from the host and reaches the user verbatim through NetError::Rejected (member.rs:221-222), limited only by the 1 MiB frame size.
refined_fix: Never release a seq whose signed event was sent. On ok:false (any reason, and after the 5 gap retries), keep that same signed event in inflight without re-signing, stop retrying on this link, and resend it after the next Welcome from any host. Release the seq only when the local state also rejects that exact event (re-run state.check: Verdict::Reject). Validation is deterministic, so no honest replica could store it. Map host reasons to a fixed set of user messages, or truncate to 200 chars and strip control characters. N2's retryable publish throttle depends on this.

title: Author equivocation is silently dropped as Stale and never detected, so honest members diverge permanently
scenario: M signs two different events E1 and E2 with the same (M, seq). It publishes E1 through the current host. Later, when M hosts (online first, or for members who cold-open to it, or after S1), it serves E2 to members who were offline. Validation returns Stale for whichever arrives second (state.rs:567-569; host.rs:863-866 only logs 'conflicts'). Heads, SyncHave and VvDigest compare only (author, seq) (sync.rs:30-49), so the fork is never found. Members show different content for that seq forever: a different message, a Delete only some replicas applied, or an InviteCreate or InviteRevoke only some see.
fix: Detect it: on Stale where seq equals a stored seq but the EventId differs, keep both signed events as an equivocation proof and propagate it (a new Ctl variant, or both events in Events). Resolve deterministically once the proof is known: mark the author as equivocating, hide both events, and drop the author's events from seq n onward. Rebuild with ConvState::rebuild, which is deterministic, so every replica converges once it has the proof. Also put per-author head EventIds into VvDigest so the periodic digest finds forks.
verdict: Could not refute; this hits 'honest members must not diverge'. A second event for an existing (author, seq) is Stale (state.rs:566-569), and PendingBuffer::ingest drops it silently (state.rs:940). At the host, member_publish only logs 'conflicts' (host.rs:863-866). Heads, missing_in and digest compare only (author, seq) (sync.rs:30-49), so the fork is never detected. M can get two versions out by hosting for members who were offline, or by publishing E1 and E2 through two solo hosts during a partition before they merge. The state.rs header (lines 72-74) admits the limitation, but that does not take it out of the threat model.
refined_fix: Now, detection only: in Replica::ingest, when the verdict is Stale and storage has no event with this id, load events_range(author, seq, seq). If a stored event has a different id, keep both signed events as a proof, log it, emit an app event that flags the author, and forward the incoming event to the host or peers so the proof spreads. Both signatures can be verified. Fold the head EventId of each author into the VvDigest input so the 60 s digest exposes forks. Follow-up (wire and semantics): resolve deterministically once a proof is known. Mark the author as equivocating, hide both events and drop the author's events from seq n on, rebuilding with ConvState::rebuild so every replica converges. This needs a proof Ctl variant or a rule that carries both events in Events.

title: The roster's voice field comes from self-reported Status while the SFU forwards by VoiceJoin, allowing invisible listening
scenario: M sends Ctl::VoiceJoin{channel: room}, and the SFU forwards that room's audio to M (sfu.rs:444-455, 101, 370). M keeps reporting Status{voice: None}. The roster everyone sees is built from m.status.voice (host.rs:323), so the room shows no new participant, and M listens to the whole voice room invisibly. Conversely, Status{voice: Some(room)} without VoiceJoin shows a ghost participant. voice_active for proactive migration (host.rs:1014) is wrong in both cases. muted and deafened are also only cosmetic: M can appear muted while talking.
fix: At the host, derive RosterEntry.voice for members from the SFU's per-member voice, which only VoiceJoin and VoiceLeave set. Add Sfu::voice_of(user), use it in build_roster, call mark_roster when VoiceJoin or VoiceLeave changes it, and ignore Status.voice at the host. Optionally derive a 'speaking' indicator from the SFU uplink stats rather than trusting muted.
verdict: Not refuted, though it falls outside the five listed must-nots; kept as a judgment call. Room forwarding follows SFU state set only by VoiceJoin and VoiceLeave (sfu.rs:101, 370, 444-463). The roster everyone sees takes voice from the member's own Status (host.rs:323), and the host never compares the two. M can VoiceJoin without setting Status.voice and receive the whole room's audio while invisible. The reverse gives a ghost participant. Honest members rely on the roster to know who hears them, and the fix is local. Proactive migration's voice_active (host.rs:1013-1014) uses the same field. A ghost can only block a migration, which is harmless; an invisible listener cannot hide honest participants. muted and deafened are cosmetic by nature.
refined_fix: Add Sfu::voice_of(&UserId) -> Option<ChannelId>. In build_roster, fill RosterEntry.voice for members from ctx.net.media.sfu(&server) and ignore Status.voice at the host. When VoiceJoin or VoiceLeave changes m.voice, have the SFU try_send SessionCmd::StatusChanged, which already calls mark_roster for hosts (mod.rs:582-585). voice_active then follows the SFU automatically. Optional: derive a 'speaking' indicator from SFU uplink stats.

title: Any current or former member can permanently pin the rendezvous record (seq exhaustion, published_ms in the future)
scenario: rdv_sk is derived from server_secret and never rotated, so ex-members can still sign. A signer publishes a valid record with timestamp/seq at or near i64::MAX and published_ms = u64::MAX, naming itself as host. Honest publishers compute next_seq = max(now, seen + 1) (rdv.rs:94-99, 346), and i64::try_from then fails in record_packet (rdv.rs:107), so every publish returns Published::Failed. The DHT and the relay keep the higher seq, so cold joiners and solo hosts resolve the attacker's record. A published_ms in the future makes it count as fresh forever (rdv.rs:342, 556): solo hosts keep deferring (the force path fails the same way), and hosts re-dial the attacker on every resolve (wake_from_record). Joiners whose bootstrap peers are offline are sent only to the attacker, who acts as a rogue host for newcomers, or to nobody.
fix: In Latest::note and resolve_first, ignore packets with timestamp > now + 10 min and records with published_ms > now + 5 min: treat them as invalid and exclude them from max_seq. Count a record as fresh only when now - published_ms is within [0, 15 min]. If the only higher seq is a far-future one, still publish at now_us (log that rdv is degraded). Document that rdv is best effort and that ex-members keep write access until a server_secret rotation exists.
verdict: Could not refute. rdv_sk is derived from server_secret, which every current and former member holds. Latest::note keeps the highest seq from any validly signed packet, readable or not, with no future check (rdv.rs:167-181). publish computes next_seq = max(now, seen + 1) (rdv.rs:94-99, 346), and record_packet fails on i64::try_from (rdv.rs:107), so after a record at seq i64::MAX every honest publish returns Failed and is retried every 60 s (rdv.rs:544-547). published_ms = u64::MAX satisfies `now - published_ms < 15 min` forever because saturating_sub gives 0 (rdv.rs:342, 556). The clobber rule therefore defers to the attacker, and periodic resolves keep waking dials to it (wake_from_record). resolve_first returns that record to cold joiners (rdv.rs:286-316). Hedged: BEP44 nodes keep the highest seq; whether the n0 pkarr relay rejects far-future timestamps was not checked, but the DHT path is enough. Rendezvous is only a hint, but a single signer can pin it for good, and joiners whose bootstrap peers are offline are sent to the attacker.
refined_fix: In Latest::note and resolve_first, ignore packets with timestamp > now + 10 min and records with published_ms > now + 5 min: treat them as invalid and leave them out of max_seq and dht_seq. Count a record as fresh only when now - published_ms is within [0, 15 min]. If the only higher seq is a far-future one, publish at now_us without CAS and log that rendezvous is degraded. Document that ex-members keep rendezvous write access until server_secret rotation exists.

title: Members accept arbitrary roster contents from the host (non-members, unbounded size), which poisons storage and the next host's short ids
scenario: M, as host, broadcasts Roster frames of up to 1 MiB (about 5,000 entries) listing random non-member UserIds with addresses, a new set each time. member.rs:111-115 only checks host and epoch. For every entry, note_roster (mod.rs:1323-1349) calls learn_hint (adding a MemoryLookup entry), writes a persist_peer storage row and calls dm.peers_seen. It also persists the roster as last_roster. When an honest member later becomes host, become_host inherits short ids from that roster without any membership check (mod.rs:1044-1051). With 16,383 fake entries every id is taken, and alloc_short_id (mod.rs:1456-1459) returns MAX_SHORT_ID to every new member. The result is duplicate track ids: voices mixed in jitter buffers, two sharers' uploads merged into one VideoTrack, and keyframe and bitrate messages sent to the wrong member.
fix: In note_roster, drop entries whose user is not ConvState::is_member, refuse rosters with more than about 256 entries, and do not persist non-members. In become_host, inherit only entries of current members, capped at the member count. Make alloc_short_id return Option: when ids are exhausted, the host rejects the member or reclaims the id of the longest-offline user instead of handing out a duplicate.
verdict: Could not refute. Members check only roster.host and epoch (member.rs:111-115). note_roster calls learn_hint, persist_peer (a storage row) and dm.peers_seen for every entry, with no membership check and no size cap (mod.rs:1323-1349). A host can send about 16k entries in one roster frame (estimate: about 50 B per entry, under MAX_FRAME 1 MiB), and new random sets add storage rows without bound. become_host inherits short ids from the inherited roster and last_roster without checking membership (mod.rs:1044-1051). The malicious host also controls the succession list, so the successor that promotes after M leaves uses M's roster. Once all of 1..=MAX_SHORT_ID (0x3FFF) are taken, alloc_short_id returns MAX_SHORT_ID to every member (mod.rs:1456-1459). The result is duplicate track ids: mixed voices, merged uploads, and keyframe or bitrate messages sent to the wrong member.
refined_fix: In note_roster, refuse rosters with more than about 256 entries and skip entries whose user is not ConvState::is_member: no learn_hint, no persist_peer, no peers_seen, and drop them from the persisted copy. In become_host, inherit short ids only for current members, capped at the member count. Make alloc_short_id return Option<u16>. When ids run out, reclaim the id of the longest-offline inherited user, or reject the joining member; never hand out a duplicate.

title: Per-member Have set and clip list are unbounded and unvalidated
scenario: M sends Ctl::Have{add: about 32,000 random hashes, remove: []} frames of 1 MiB each, continuously. m.have grows by about 1.3 MB of heap per frame with no limit for as long as the link lives (host.rs:774-781). holders() then lists M for any hash, so downloads try M first and fail over. Hello.have and Hello.clips are taken in the same way (host.rs:377-378). ClipInfo fields are never validated, and the clips list is never capped.
fix: Cap each member's have at about 20,000 hashes and ignore adds beyond that. Accept only hashes that appear as attachment hashes in ConvState or as announced clip hashes. Cap clips at about 200 entries and validate ClipInfo (name <= 100 chars, size <= 5 MB, duration <= 20 s). Apply the same caps to Hello.
verdict: Could not refute; this violates the 'no unbounded memory' must-not. Have.add is inserted into the member's HashSet with no limit for as long as the link lives (host.rs:774-781). One 1 MiB frame holds about 32k hashes, or about 1.3 MB of heap (estimate), and frames can repeat without limit. Hello.have and Hello.clips are bounded only by the frame size (host.rs:377-378). ClipInfo is never validated. holders() then lists M for any hash it claims (host.rs:244-257), so downloads try M first.
refined_fix: Cap each member's have at about 20,000 hashes and ignore adds beyond that. Cap clips at about 200 entries. Validate ClipInfo: name at most MAX_NAME_CHARS (100) with no control characters, size at most 5 MB, duration at most 20 s, per architecture.md. Apply the same caps to Hello.have and Hello.clips in accept_member.

title: Junk Events from a member fill and evict the shared pending buffer (non-member authors are buffered as Gap)
scenario: M sends Events frames full of events signed by freshly generated non-member keys (seq 1, valid shape). The membership check returns Gap for non-members (state.rs:605-607), so each one is buffered (host.rs:752-756, then ingest_signed). About 10,000 junk events evict, oldest first (state.rs:873-880), honest events waiting for a prerequisite: for example a joiner's events that arrived before its admit, or an out-of-order sync page. That stalls convergence until the next resync, which is at most every 30 s. Each junk event also costs an ed25519 verify on the session actor.
fix: On member links, accept Events only from authors who are members or who are admitted by an event in the same batch. Tag pending entries with their source link, cap each source (e.g. 1,000) and evict that source's own entries first. Drop a source's entries when its link closes.
verdict: Narrowed. The eviction sub-claim is real but transient. Events from non-member authors are Live Gaps (state.rs:604-607) and are buffered (host.rs:752-756 -> ingest_signed), so they evict honest pending events oldest-first (state.rs:873-880). Resync brings those back within about 30-60 s, comparable to a bad link. The CPU sub-claim survives and does not depend on membership: ingest_signed verifies every event's ed25519 signature on the single session actor before validation (mod.rs:1273), so replaying already-stored history costs the same and is then dropped as Stale. Estimate: about 7,000 small events per 1 MiB frame, about 0.2-0.35 s of CPU per frame. The session-wide LINK_QUEUE of 1024 decoded frames (mod.rs:327) lets one member's backlog delay every other member's frames, including Ticks. If that delay passes host_dead (10 s), the host drops honest members as silent (host.rs:981-984). Holding 1024 queued 1 MiB frames is up to about 1 GiB (estimate).
refined_fix: Give each member link an ingest budget for Events and Publish (for example events/s and bytes/s, enforced in the link reader or before ingest_signed). Over the budget, pause reading that link; never drop honest members. Tag pending entries with their source link, cap each source at about 1,000, evict that source's own entries first, and drop them when its link closes. Optionally drop non-member-authored events unless the batch or the pending set contains their MemberAdmit. Make the shared link_tx fair per link (see N2).

title: Member side accepts any 'by' in host-relayed SoundPlayed and Typing, so a malicious host can impersonate members
scenario: M, as host, sends SoundPlayed{by: Alice, clip: a clip M controls} and Typing{by: Alice} to its members. voice.rs:503-506 and member.rs:156-160 accept any by other than me. Members see 'Alice is typing' and 'Alice played X', and fetch the clip from the named holder. Members cannot do this through an honest host, which checks by == sender (host.rs:791, sfu.rs:506).
fix: Have SoundPlayed carry an ed25519 signature by 'by' over ("tincan-sound1", server, clip.hash, ts), and verify it at receivers. Sign Typing the same way, or document it as an ephemeral, host-vouched residual. At minimum, receivers should drop any by that is not a current member present in the roster.
verdict: Could not refute; this is impersonation in a control message (a must-not). Members emit Typing for any by other than themselves (member.rs:156-160), and voice sessions emit SoundPlayed for any by other than themselves, from the host and from call peers alike (voice.rs:503-507). Only an honest host checks by == sender (host.rs:791; sfu.rs:506). A malicious host, or a call peer, can show 'Alice played X', with a clip it picked, and 'Alice is typing'.
refined_fix: Now: receivers drop Typing and SoundPlayed whose by is not ConvState::is_member and present in the current roster's online list. In calls and DMs, require by == the peer. Follow-up (wire): SoundPlayed carries an ed25519 signature by `by` over ("tincan-sound1", server, clip.hash, ts) with a freshness window, checked by the host and by receivers. Typing gets signed the same way, or is documented as a host-vouched residual.

title: SoundPlayed is forwarded to the room without validation or rate limit
scenario: M, in a voice room, sends SoundPlayed{by: M, clip: ClipInfo{name: a 500 KB string, size: u64::MAX, duration_ms: u32::MAX}} hundreds of times per second. The host forwards each copy to every room member's live queue (sfu.rs:512-517). Each member emits NetEvent::SoundPlayed ('Heard in this call') and may start fetching from M. This fills live queues (see N2) and floods the UI.
fix: Validate ClipInfo at the host and at receivers (name <= 100 chars, size <= 5 MB, duration <= 20 s). Allow at most one SoundPlayed per member per 2 s, and dedupe by hash within 30 s.
verdict: Could not refute. The SFU checks only by == member and room membership, then sends every SoundPlayed to each room member over the CtlTx live queue (sfu.rs:506-521). It does no ClipInfo validation, rate limiting or dedupe. Receivers emit NetEvent::SoundPlayed for each one (voice.rs:503-507). Flooding fills members' live queues, and the next broadcast() then closes them as 'too slow' (host.rs:229-232), the same split mechanism as N2. It also floods the UI with oversized names.
refined_fix: At the host, validate ClipInfo: name at most 100 chars with no control characters, size at most 5 MB, duration at most 20 s. Allow at most one SoundPlayed per member per 2 s and dedupe by hash within 30 s. Receivers validate as well. Treat SoundPlayed as droppable on a full queue (see N2).

title: Admissions are not rate-limited, and default invites have unlimited uses
scenario: An invite holder, or any member (who can mint unlimited InviteCreate; create_invite defaults to max_uses 0, net.rs:239), scripts JoinRequests with thousands of fresh identities. Each passes verify_join_request and makes the host author a permanent MemberAdmit plus a Profile event (host.rs:475-494). Every member stores these forever, since v1 has no kick. Membership inflates, and the identities supply Sybil attesters for S1.
fix: Rate-limit admissions per invite_pk (e.g. 1 per 10 s, 20 per hour) and per host. Default create_invite to a small max_uses (e.g. 10), with an explicit 'unlimited' option. Show join bursts in the UI.
verdict: Narrowed. That any member may admit is by design (state.rs:64-66), but nothing bounds the rate. admit_joiner has no limit (host.rs:453-496), and create_invite defaults to unlimited uses (net.rs:239). An extra path skips JoinRequests entirely. Any member may author MemberAdmit for a known invite, so Publish passes member_publish (state.rs:643-647; host.rs:839-861). The Sybil-signed Profile events then arrive through Events (host.rs:752-756). Each Sybil adds an author to Heads, about 33 B each (estimate). At roughly 31k authors (estimate) SyncHave no longer fits MAX_FRAME (wire.rs:17), and link::encode drops it while Link::send still returns true (link.rs:39-47, 249-254). After that, no new link syncs history, members never reach sync_out_done and cannot publish, server-wide. Sybils also feed S1's attestation counts.
refined_fix: Host-side policy (not validation, so replicas cannot diverge): rate-limit admissions per invite_pk (for example 1 per 10 s, 20 per hour) and per server (for example 60 per hour). Apply the same budget to MemberAdmit events published by members and to the first event of any author new to this replica arriving through Publish or Events. Answer with a retryable refusal that relies on N9's never-release rule. Default create_invite to max_uses 10, with an explicit 'unlimited' option. Make SyncHave scale with membership: send Heads in several frames with a final marker, so membership size can never hit the frame cap.

title: Video group reordering keeps unlimited pending groups and drains them recursively, so one stream sequence crashes the process with a stack overflow
scenario: The uploader opens a GOP stream for its own screen track (the host's Upload sink accepts it, sfu.rs:641), sends one keyframe and never finishes that stream. It then opens 20k more uni streams with increasing group_seq. Each gets a 9-byte header, one 6-byte frame and FIN. In on_msg (recv.rs:251-261) every new group gets a fresh Pending (since=now, 1 frame, want_key false), so nothing switches and `pending` grows without limit. Msg::End for each one only sets ended=true (269-272). Stream credit comes back as each stream finishes, so 100 concurrent streams is not a cap. The attacker then finishes the first stream: end_current -> switch -> end_current -> switch ... (recv.rs:216-236) recurses once per pending group. next_pending and the stale scan also make this O(n^2). I reproduced it with a standalone copy of the logic on a 2 MiB thread (tokio's default worker stack; nothing in the repo sets thread_stack_size): 5k groups drained in 40 ms, 20k groups gave 'thread has overflowed its stack' and the process aborted. Result: one malicious member kills the host (every hosted server, DM and call goes down) and can do it again to each successor. A malicious host can do the same to members (SessionSink accepts any screen track, voice.rs:668), and so can a call peer during an active call. Large frames held in pending also make it an unbounded-memory attack.
fix: In on_msg, cap pending groups per track (for example 2). When a new group arrives and pending.len() >= 2, switch to it, or drop the oldest pending group and report a gap. Ignore any group_seq more than 16 ahead of cur. Rewrite switch/end_current as a loop ('while let Some(next) = ...'). Drop a pending group that has ended with no frames.
verdict: Confirmed by reading the code. Every member link at the host gets spawn_video_rx with an Upload sink (sfu.rs:165), and that sink accepts the member's own screen track (sfu.rs:641). After the first group's keyframe is delivered, want_key is false and cur_ended stays false while that stream is open. read_stream only has a timeout for the header (recv.rs:106), so the stream can stay open forever. Each later group creates a fresh Pending with since=now and one frame. The switch condition (recv.rs:256) only checks the group that just got a frame, so no switch happens and `pending` grows with no limit. Msg::End only sets ended (269-272), and stream credit comes back once each reader finishes. Finishing the first stream then runs end_current -> switch -> end_current recursively, one level per pending group (216-236). Each level also does an O(n) next_pending and stale scan, so the drain is O(n^2). Nothing sets thread_stack_size (grep is empty), so tokio's 2 MiB worker stacks apply. Pending frames also hold attacker data without a bound. A malicious host (SessionSink accepts any screen track, voice.rs:668) or a call peer can do the same to a member.
refined_fix: recv.rs: (1) In on_msg, cap pending groups per track at 2-4. When a new group would go over the cap, switch to the oldest pending group (abandoning the current one, which already reports a gap) instead of inserting. Ignore any group_seq more than 16 ahead of cur. (2) Cap frames and bytes per pending group (PENDING_MAX frames already exists; add about 2 MiB) and switch when the cap is reached. (3) Apply the SWITCH_AFTER check to the oldest pending group's `since` on every Frame/End for the track, not only to the group that just got a frame. (4) Make the switch/end_current chain a loop: `let mut next = Some(g); while let Some(g) = next.take() { ...deliver...; if p.ended { self.cur_ended = true; next = self.next_pending(); if next.is_none() && p.reset { want_key = true; gap } } }`. (5) Use pending.range(..) for next_pending and the stale removal instead of full scans.

title: Every SyncHave spawns a full-history send_missing task, with no coalescing or rate limit (host, member, probe and DM paths)
scenario: A member sends Ctl::SyncHave{heads: []} (a few bytes) in a loop. Each one runs ctx.spawn_sync (mod.rs:1231-1242), a new task that streams the whole server history from SQLite in 256 KiB pages (replica.rs:150-209). The 30 s limit at host.rs:761 only covers the host's own SyncHave reply, not the spawn. If the attacker reads its stream, a ~10-byte frame costs the host several MB of storage reads and upload (100 frames/s = 100 full histories/s of disk, CPU and uplink). If it stops reading, the bulk queue (2) fills and every task blocks in send_bulk while holding a 256 KiB page plus a batch of up to 256 events, so tasks and memory grow without bound until OOM. The same pattern exists at host.rs:937-941 (probe link), member.rs:130-133 (a malicious host against members) and dm.rs:493-504/529/536 (any DM peer through DmHello/SyncHave, including strangers).
fix: Allow at most one outstanding sync per link: keep `sync_running: bool` and `queued: Option<Heads>`, replace queued with the latest heads, and start it on LinkEvent::SyncSent (the DM path needs a matching completion signal). On the host, also enforce a per-UserId minimum of 10 s between full syncs that survives reconnects, and close the link after more than 10 SyncHave per minute. Apply the same guard in member.rs, the probe link and dm.rs on_heads.
verdict: Confirmed. host.rs:757-758 calls ctx.spawn_sync for every SyncHave. spawn_sync (mod.rs:1231-1242) starts a new send_missing task each time, with no in-flight check. The 30 s last_sync_reply check (761) only throttles the host's own SyncHave reply. send_missing (replica.rs:150-209) plans every missing range and reads SQLite in 256-event batches. Against a reader, each 10-byte frame costs a full history of reads plus host uplink. Against a non-reader, the bulk queue (2) fills and every new task parks in send_bulk holding a page of up to 256 KiB plus its batch. Ticks alone take about 34 minutes to fill the 1024-frame live queue, and the link is only torn down when a broadcast finds that queue full, so tasks pile up until OOM. The same unguarded spawn exists on the probe link (host.rs:937-941), on a member for a malicious host (member.rs:130-133), and in dm.rs on_heads (SyncHave/DmHello). The DM case only matters for contacts with history: for a fresh stranger, missing_in is empty.
refined_fix: Track per link `sync_running: bool` plus `queued: Option<Heads>`. While a sync runs, a new SyncHave only replaces `queued`. On LinkEvent::SyncSent, start `queued` if present (DM run_conn needs the same completion signal: have its spawn send SyncSent on its own channel). On the host, also keep a per-UserId token bucket in HostState (for example a burst of 3, then 1 per 10 s) so reconnecting does not reset it. Over budget, drop the frame; after sustained abuse (more than 20 per minute), close the link. Apply the same one-in-flight guard in member.rs, on the probe link and in dm.rs on_heads.

title: Typing and SoundPlayed are fanned out to everyone with no rate limit, and the host then disconnects honest members whose queues fill
scenario: A member floods Ctl::Typing{by: self} (about 70 B): member_frame calls h.broadcast to every other member (host.rs:790-796) and emits a NetEvent per frame. broadcast closes any member whose 1024-frame live queue is full ('member too slow', host.rs:229-232). At 1 MB/s from the attacker the host has to upload N MB/s, which saturates a home uplink, so every honest member's queue fills in well under a second and gets closed. They reconnect and are dropped again, so the server becomes unusable. SoundPlayed (sfu.rs:506-521) is worse. ClipInfo.name is an unbounded String (wire.rs:31-40), so one frame can be about 1 MiB. It is re-encoded per room member (CtlTx::send) and queued with try_send, and the live queue is bounded in frames, not bytes (link.rs:32, 249-257), so each member link can hold 1024 x 1 MiB = 1 GiB on the host. The queues it fills make the next Tick or Events broadcast close those members. The same 1 MiB names are cloned into NetEvent::SoundPlayed on the host and on every listener; the 4096-slot event bus (inner.rs:35) keeps them while the app lags, so up to about 4 GiB.
fix: Add per-member token buckets in HostState keyed by UserId so they survive reconnects: Typing at 1/s burst 3, coalesced per channel; SoundPlayed at 1/s burst 3. Drop excess silently. Validate payload sizes on decode with a tincan-core `Ctl::check_limits` called in FrameReader: ClipInfo.name <= 100 chars, Status.app_version <= 32, Reject.reason <= 256, and so on. Bound the live queue in bytes (for example 4 MiB per link). Never close a member because frames relayed from another member filled its queue: drop those relayed frames instead.
verdict: Confirmed. Typing (host.rs:790-796) only checks by==user, then calls h.broadcast to every member and emits a NetEvent per frame, with no rate limit. broadcast closes any member whose 1024-frame live queue is full (host.rs:229-232). Fan-out of N x the attacker's rate saturates the host uplink, honest queues fill, and those members are dropped as 'too slow' over and over. SoundPlayed (sfu.rs:506-521) needs the sender in a room, but VoiceJoin for any live voice channel is always accepted. ClipInfo.name is an unbounded String (core wire.rs:31-40), so one frame can be about 1 MiB. CtlTx::send re-encodes it per room member and try_sends it onto that member's live queue, which is bounded in frames, not bytes (link.rs:32, 257), so each link can queue about 1 GiB. The next Tick or Events broadcast then closes those members. NetEvent::SoundPlayed copies (host and every listener via voice.rs:503-506) sit in the 4096-slot bus while the app lags.
refined_fix: (1) In HostState, keyed by UserId so reconnects do not reset them: Typing at 1/s burst 3 (drop excess, optionally coalesce per channel); SoundPlayed at 1/s burst 3, checked in Sfu::on_ctl (the SFU needs a small map too). (2) Add size limits in tincan-core applied on decode (a `Ctl::check_limits` called in FrameReader::next, with the same check in send paths): ClipInfo.name <= 100 chars, Status.app_version <= 32, Reject.reason <= 256, and so on. Drop or close on violation. (3) Never let relayed ephemeral frames (Typing, SoundPlayed, claim refreshes) evict session traffic: enqueue them only while the target's live queue has more than half its capacity free (`Sender::capacity()`), otherwise drop them silently, and never close a member for them. Keep closing on full only for Events/Ticks. (4) Optionally bound the live queue in bytes (for example 4 MiB per link).

title: Any member can make the host re-claim its epoch and broadcast HostMoved to all members on every HostCompare
scenario: A member sends HostCompare with a valid self-signed claim (claim.host == itself, low epoch, connected 0, score 0) over and over. compare_from_member (873-891) has no cooldown. Each time the host wins, so win_merge (640-660) signs a new claim with epoch+1, persists it with upsert_conv, broadcasts HostMoved to every member, schedules a roster and emits ConnectionChanged. Every member handles host_moved (member.rs:227-237) and emits ConnectionChanged too. Merge state is only set when the host loses, so nothing throttles the winning path. Thousands of HostCompare per second mean thousands of SQLite writes and signatures, N x HostMoved per frame (which fills live queues and leads to 'too slow' disconnects, as in DOS-03), unbounded epoch inflation, and UI event floods on every member. The S1 attestation fix does not address this.
fix: Accept at most one HostCompare per peer UserId per 60 s (a map in HostState that survives reconnects) and ignore any arriving while one is handled. If my epoch is already above theirs, reply with my current claim as HostMoved to that peer only: no new claim, no broadcast, no record write. Coalesce the epoch-refresh broadcast to my own members to at most once a minute.
verdict: Confirmed. compare_from_member (host.rs:873-891) only requires no merge or handoff in progress, a valid signature, and claim.host == sender. Any member can self-sign a claim naming itself (SignedHostClaim is signed by the host it names). merge_winner keys on (connected, epoch, score, -id) (election.rs:171), so the attacker sends connected=0, a low epoch and score=0, and the host wins every time. win_merge (640-660) then signs epoch+1, persists it with upsert_conv (update_record), broadcasts HostMoved to every member, schedules a roster and emits ConnectionChanged. Every member runs host_moved (member.rs:227-237) and emits ConnectionChanged too. Nothing records state on the winning path, so the next HostCompare does it again. That means unthrottled signatures, SQLite writes, N-fold broadcasts that fill live queues (which leads to 'too slow' drops) and UI event floods.
refined_fix: In HostState, keep last_compare: HashMap<UserId, Instant> that survives reconnects, and ignore a HostCompare from a peer that compared within the last 60 s. When I win and my current epoch is already above theirs, send my existing claim as HostMoved to that peer only: no new claim, no upsert_conv, no broadcast. Only when theirs >= mine, claim max+1. Even then, send the refresh broadcast to my own members at most once a minute, since members already accept a roster whose epoch is >= theirs.

title: The SFU forwards voice datagrams verbatim with no rate or size limit, and the forwarded flood starves every room member's control stream
scenario: A member sends VoiceJoin for any voice room (always allowed), then sends 1200-byte datagrams carrying its own valid voice track id at line rate. forward_task and forward (sfu.rs:659-669, 366-395) copy each one to every other room member (up to 9) and into the host app's audio_in. noq sends queued datagrams before stream data (docs/architecture.md, Connections), so the 16 KiB datagram buffer toward each victim is always full and their control streams (Tick, Events, Roster) get only leftover capacity. Their live queues then fill and the host closes them as 'too slow', or the members stop seeing Ticks and declare the host dead after 10 s and fail over. The host uplink carries N x the attacker's rate, which hurts everyone, not just the room, and honest speakers' packets are crowded out.
fix: Add a per-member token bucket in Sfu::forward: about 60 packets/s sustained (Opus at 20 ms is 50/s), burst 30, and drop datagrams longer than 12 + 512 bytes. Apply it before fanning out and before audio_in. Count drops and close the member link if it runs more than 5x over budget for 5 s. Optionally require increasing seq values.
verdict: Confirmed. forward_task/forward (sfu.rs:659-669, 366-395) drop only datagrams whose track is not the sender's own voice track (voice_track_from). There is no rate or size check, and any member can VoiceJoin. Each datagram goes to every other room member through Connection::send_datagram, which in noq calls datagrams().send(data, drop=true) (noq connection.rs:697) and drops the oldest queued datagrams to make room. Honest speakers' packets queued toward each victim are therefore discarded by the attacker's flood. noq writes DATAGRAM frames before STREAM frames (connection/mod.rs:6533 vs 6597), so with a permanently full 16 KiB datagram buffer the victims' control stream (Tick, Events, Roster) only gets leftover packet space. Their live queues fill (leading to 'too slow' drops), or they miss Ticks for 10 s and fail over. The host uplink carries up to 9x the attacker's rate, which hurts every server it hosts.
refined_fix: In Sfu::forward, before fan-out and before audio_in, apply a per-member token bucket stored in the SFU Member (keyed by UserId and kept across add_member replacement): about 100 packets/s sustained with a burst of 50 (Opus at 20 ms is 50/s; leave room for jitter clumping), plus a byte budget of about 128 kbit/s. Drop datagrams longer than AUDIO_HEADER_LEN + 400 bytes. Count drops, and close the member link if it stays more than 5x over budget for 5 s. Still record the uplink stats for honest-looking packets only.

title: Repeated Subscribe or KeyframeRequest re-seeds the 2 MiB GOP cache each time and leaks writer tasks that can block forever
scenario: Sfu::on_ctl Subscribe (sfu.rs:464-476) ignores the result of m.subs.insert and calls t.add_remote every time. add_remote (track.rs:382-396) spawns a new writer, seeds it with the whole cached group (up to 160 frames / 2 MiB) and replaces the old viewer. The old RemoteViewer is dropped without a flush, so its writer keeps sending everything it had queued. A modified client that never accepts uni streams leaves the host's 100 stream credits used up, so every new writer then blocks forever in conn.open_uni (track.rs:589-602; only a flush breaks that select). The attacker sends Subscribe{track} in a loop (5-byte frames): writer tasks accumulate without limit, each pinning up to 2 MiB of an older GOP after the cache rolls over (about 1.8 GB per hour at one Subscribe per second). Against a client that does read, each Subscribe makes the host upload another 2 MiB. KeyframeRequest from a viewer (viewer_wants_key, 424-444) also re-seeds from a fresh cache with no per-viewer limit, so the host's uplink toward the attacker is limited only by the attacker's downlink, not the share's bitrate. The call path at voice.rs:508-514 has the same pattern.
fix: In sfu.rs return early when `!m.subs.insert(track)`; do the same in voice.rs, ignoring Subscribe while peer_watching is already true. In add_remote, keep an existing viewer for that peer, or flush the old one and make the writer exit when its channel closes after a flush. Wrap open_uni in a 2 s timeout and break on expiry. Add a per-viewer limit in viewer_wants_key (at most one re-seed per 2 s; otherwise just set want_key). Limit Subscribe/Unsubscribe toggles to 4/s per member.
verdict: Confirmed. Sfu::on_ctl Subscribe (sfu.rs:464-476) ignores the result of m.subs.insert and calls t.add_remote every time. Subscribe has no voice or room requirement; it only needs a live track. add_remote (track.rs:382-396) spawns a new writer, seeds it with the cached group (up to 160 frames / 2 MiB) and replaces the viewer. The dropped RemoteViewer only closes its channel, and the old writer keeps writing everything it had queued. A client that never accepts uni streams (or advertises no uni credit) makes conn.open_uni block. Only a flush on that viewer's Shared breaks the select (track.rs:589-602), and once it is replaced nothing references it, so each such writer is stuck forever holding Wire clones that pin older GOP bytes. A client that does read gets another 2 MiB upload per 5-byte Subscribe. viewer_wants_key (424-444) re-seeds a subscribed viewer from a fresh cache on every KeyframeRequest, with no per-viewer limit. voice.rs:508-514 calls add_remote on every Subscribe during a call.
refined_fix: sfu.rs: `if !m.subs.insert(track) { return; }` before add_remote. voice.rs: ignore Subscribe while peer_watching is already true. track.rs: (1) In add_remote, keep an existing remote viewer for that peer instead of replacing it. (2) Give Shared a `closed` flag set (with flush.notify) when RemoteViewer drops, and have the writer return when it sees closed, including inside the open_uni select. (3) Wrap open_uni in a 2 s timeout; on expiry, flush (want_key) and continue, or end the writer. (4) In viewer_wants_key, allow at most one cache re-seed per viewer per 2 s; otherwise only flush and set want_key, and let the coalesced upstream request handle it. Optionally limit Subscribe/Unsubscribe toggles to about 4/s per member (keyed by UserId).

title: Video ingress allows 8 MiB per stream across 100 streams, decodes tiny frames in quadratic time, and does not police a sharer that ignores its target
scenario: (a) Memory: read_stream accumulates each stream in VideoFrameReader up to MAX_VIDEO_FRAME = 8 MiB plus one chunk (core media.rs:201, 213). There is no per-frame deadline, and the transport allows 100 concurrent uni streams. A member opens 100 streams for its own track, declares 8 MiB frames and never completes them, so the host holds about 800 MiB per member link (and members hold the same for a malicious host). (b) CPU: VideoFrameReader::next calls buf.drain(..) per frame (media.rs:231), which is quadratic. I measured about 3 ms per 64 KiB chunk of minimal 6-byte frames (11k frames per chunk). Each of those frames then goes through an mpsc hop, upload_track, Wire::encode and a per-viewer enqueue and write, so about 1 MB/s of tiny frames (about 170k frames/s) can saturate the 3-worker runtime. (c) Rate: overloaded() budgets 250 ms of the measured input rate (track.rs:161-164, 319), and TargetBitrate is only advisory. A sharer sending 50 Mbps is forwarded at 50 Mbps to every viewer until their links congest, which saturates the host uplink for everyone.
fix: Give VideoFrameReader a read offset with occasional compaction (as FrameDecoder does), or use BytesMut::split_to. Lower MAX_VIDEO_FRAME for screen tracks to 2 MiB. Limit concurrent readers per connection (for example 4 per track and 8 in total; stop the rest) and add a 2 s timeout for completing a frame. At the SFU, police each track's ingress with a token bucket at max(1.5 x the last target, VIDEO_MIN_BPS) bytes/s and at most 60 frames/s, dropping deltas until the next keyframe when exceeded. Derive the viewer queue budget from the cap, not from the measured input.
verdict: (a) Confirmed. read_stream accumulates each stream in VideoFrameReader up to MAX_VIDEO_FRAME = 8 MiB (core media.rs:201, 213). The app keeps reading, so QUIC flow control does not limit it, and there is no deadline after the header. The defaults allow 100 concurrent uni streams, so a member can keep about 800 MiB live per link at the host; a malicious host or call peer can do the same to a member. (b) Partly confirmed. drain(..) per frame (media.rs:231) makes each 64 KiB chunk of tiny frames O(chunk^2/frame), not unbounded, and every frame then goes through the mpsc hop, upload_track (SFU lock), Wire::encode and per-viewer offer, so CPU cost per input byte is high. (c) Confirmed. Nothing polices ingress: TargetBitrate is advisory, and overloaded() budgets 250 ms of the measured input (track.rs:161-164, 319), so a 50 Mbps sharer is forwarded at whatever each viewer's congestion window allows, saturating the host uplink for every session.
refined_fix: (1) VideoFrameReader: keep a read offset and compact occasionally (like FrameDecoder), or use BytesMut::split_to. (2) Lower the screen-track frame limit to 2 MiB. (3) In video_rx, limit concurrent readers per connection (for example 4 per track, 8 total) and stop extras with VIDEO_REFUSED. Give each frame a completion deadline (no progress or no complete frame within 2 s: stop the stream). (4) In the host Upload sink, before VideoTrack::push, police ingress per track with a token bucket at about 1.5 x VIDEO_MAX_BPS and a burst of one keyframe (about 2 MiB), and at most 60 frames/s. When over budget, drop deltas until the next keyframe and call gap(). Police at the mode cap rather than the AIMD target, so an honest encoder's lag after a decrease is not punished. Derive the viewer queue byte budget from that cap, not from the measured input rate.

title: Endpoint-wide QUIC defaults let a peer park about 250 MB per connection in streams nobody accepts (DM strangers included)
scenario: transport_config only sets keep-alive, datagram buffers and idle timeout. noq/iroh defaults therefore apply: 100 concurrent bidi and 100 uni streams with a 1.25 MB stream_receive_window each, and an unlimited connection receive_window (noq-proto config/transport.rs:566-580). The app accepts exactly one bidi stream per server or DM connection, and accepts uni streams only where a video reader runs. Any peer can open the other 99 bidi streams, plus 100 uni streams on a DM link outside a call (or a member link outside voice), and fill each with 1.25 MB that QUIC buffers indefinitely. A stranger with no shared server passes the DM check (dm.rs:435-456) and keeps the link alive by sending any frame within 120 s (dm.rs:468-489), so each throwaway identity costs about 250 MB of the victim's memory, with no global limit. Pre-auth server connections also get up to 4 s (proto.rs:17-25) with a 1 MiB first frame, and the Router does not limit concurrent handshakes.
fix: In transport_config set receive_window to about 16 MiB, stream_receive_window to 1 MiB, max_concurrent_bidi_streams to about 8 and max_concurrent_uni_streams to about 16, and confirm iroh-blobs still performs (the config is endpoint-wide). In Link::spawn for server and DM links, add a loop that accepts extra bidi streams (and uni streams where no video reader runs) and stops them at once. In proto.rs, add a global semaphore of about 64 for connections still waiting for a first frame, allow one pending connection per remote id, and limit the first frame to 256 KiB.
